content: Both type I and type II complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS) share identical diagnostic criteria. These criteria include the presence of spontaneous pain that is not confined to the distribution of a single nerve and is disproportionate to the inciting event. Additionally, there must be a history of edema, abnormal skin blood flow, or abnormal sweating in the region of the pain since the inciting event. Importantly, no other medical condition should be able to explain the severity of the pain and dysfunction observed. The primary distinction between the two types lies in the nature of the inciting event. Type I CRPS, also known as reflex sympathetic dystrophy, develops following an initiating noxious event, which may or may not involve trauma. In contrast, type II CRPS, also referred to as causalgia, arises specifically after a nerve injury.
